\[
x+b\sqrt{-1}=(u+v\sqrt{-1})^{n}
\]
be the corresponding factorization.  Since \(\gcd(x,by)=1\) and \(y\) is odd, the two conjugate factors are coprime in the ring of integers, and hence each is an \(n\)-th power.  Taking the difference of the two conjugates gives
\[
\frac{(u+v\sqrt{-1})^{n}-(u-v\sqrt{-1})^{n}}{2v\sqrt{-1}}=\frac{b}{v}.
\]
The left hand side is the \(n\)-th term of a Lucas sequence.  Thus every prime divisor of this term is either a divisor of \(n\), or a primitive divisor of the corresponding Lucas number.  By the theorem of Bilu, Hanrot and Voutier, for \(n>30\) such a primitive divisor must exist.  Comparing its congruence properties with the prime divisors of \(b\) yields a contradiction. Let \(d=d(n)\) be a positive integer such that \(dn\) is even, and let

The first asymptotic formula was obtained for fixed \(d\) by Bender and
Canfield and, independently, by Wormald.  Their result states that, as
\(n\to\infty\),
\[
 |G(n,d)| \sim
 \frac{(dn)!}{(dn/2)!2^{dn/2}(d!)^n}
 \exp\left(-\frac{d^2-1}{4}\right).
\]
McKay extended this estimate to degrees satisfying \(d=o(n^{1/3})\),
showing that the same main term is accompanied by a more refined
exponential correction.  In particular,
\[
 |G(n,d)| =
 \frac{(dn)!}{(dn/2)!2^{dn/2}(d!)^n}
 \exp\left(-\frac{d^2-1}{4}
          -\frac{d^3}{12n}
          +O\left(\frac{d^2}{n}\right)\right),
\]
uniformly in the stated range.

For larger degrees one may use complementation, since a \(d\)-regular
graph on \(n\) vertices corresponds to an \((n-1-d)\)-regular graph.
Thus the sparse estimates also cover the case \(n-1-d=o(n^{1/3})\).
The remaining range, in which both \(d\) and \(n-d\) grow proportionally
to \(n\), requires different methods, typically based on saddle-point
analysis or estimates for dense \(0\)-\(1\) matrices with prescribed
row and column sums.

We will use the following basic properties of stable polynomials. If

variables to real numbers, differentiating with respect to variables, or
taking limits (provided the resulting polynomial is not identically zero) is
stable. In particular, if $f$ is stable then so is
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} f
\]
whenever this derivative is not zero. Moreover, if $f$ has real coefficients,
then specialization at real values preserves real stability.

A polynomial with real coefficients is called \emph{real stable} if it is
stable. Equivalently, a polynomial $f\in\R[\z]$ is real stable if
\[
f(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\neq 0
\]
whenever $\Im(z_i)>0$ for all $i\in[n]$. For univariate polynomials this is
precisely the property of having only real zeros. Thus real stability is a
natural multivariate generalization of real-rootedness.

In what follows we shall be interested in maximal arithmetic hyperbolic reflection groups.  If $\Gamma$ is an arithmetic reflection group, then its commensurator
\[
\Comm(\Gamma)=\{g\in H\mid \Gamma\cap g\Gamma g^{-1}\hbox{ has finite index in both }\Gamma\hbox{ and }g\Gamma g^{-1}\}
\]
is a lattice containing $\Gamma$; moreover, by Margulis' arithmeticity/commensurator theorem, in the arithmetic case it is a dense subgroup only in the non-arithmetic case, while for arithmetic lattices the commensurator is the largest arithmetic subgroup in the corresponding commensurability class. Thus every arithmetic reflection group is contained in a maximal arithmetic lattice, and a maximal arithmetic reflection group is obtained by taking, among the reflection subgroups in its commensurability class, one which is maximal with respect to inclusion.

We shall often pass from a reflection group to its fundamental polyhedron. Consequently the study of maximal reflection groups may be phrased as the study of Coxeter polyhedra which admit no non-trivial Coxeter decomposition.

We consider the problem
\[
\left\{
\begin{array}{ll}
-\Delta u+a(x)u=|u|^{p-2}u, & \quad x\in \Omega,\\
u\in H_0^1(\Omega),
\end{array}
\right.
\]
where \(2<p<2^*\) if \(N\geq 3\), and \(2<p<+\infty\) if \(N=1,2\). The associated functional is defined on \(H_0^1(\Omega)\) by
\[
I(u)=\frac12\int_\Omega \left(|\nabla u|^2+a(x)u^2\right)\,dx
-\frac1p\int_\Omega |u|^p\,dx .
\]
We shall look for critical points of \(I\). Notice that, under the assumptions above, the quadratic form
\[
\|u\|^2=\int_\Omega \left(|\nabla u|^2+a(x)u^2\right)\,dx
\]
defines a norm equivalent to the usual norm of \(H_0^1(\Omega)\) whenever the Poincaré inequality holds in \(\Omega\); in the general case we shall simply work in the Hilbert space obtained as the completion of \(C_0^\infty(\Omega)\) with respect to this norm.

Let
\[
S=\inf\left\{\int_\Omega \left(|\nabla u|^2+a(x)u^2\right)\,dx:
u\in H_0^1(\Omega),\ |u|_p=1\right\}.
\]
Then \(S>0\), and a minimizer for \(S\), if it exists, gives rise, after a suitable normalization, to a positive solution of the equation above. Indeed, if \(u\) realizes \(S\), the Euler equation yields
\[
-\Delta u+a(x)u=S |u|^{p-2}u,
\]
and \(S^{1/(p-2)}u\) is a solution.

We shall prove that the infimum is achieved under a compactness condition which prevents loss of mass at infinity. More precisely, we assume that the embedding
\[
H_0^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^p(\Omega)
\]
is compact, or, more generally, that every minimizing sequence for \(S\) is tight in \(L^p(\Omega)\). Under this hypothesis the direct method of the calculus of variations applies. Let \((u_n)\) be a minimizing sequence with \(|u_n|_p=1\). Then \((u_n)\) is bounded in the above norm; hence, up to a subsequence,
\[
u_n\rightharpoonup u \quad \hbox{weakly in } H_0^1(\Omega),
\]
and
\[
u_n\to u \quad \hbox{strongly in } L^p(\Omega).
\]
Thus \(|u|_p=1\), and by weak lower semicontinuity
\[
\int_\Omega \left(|\nabla u|^2+a(x)u^2\right)\,dx\leq S.
\]
Consequently \(u\) is a minimizer. By replacing \(u\) with \(|u|\) and using the strong maximum principle, one obtains a non-negative, and in fact positive, solution in each connected component where it is not identically zero.

\tag{2.1}
\]
where \(p>1\). We say that \(u\) is a solution of (2.1) if \(u\in H^1_0(\Omega)\cap L^\infty(\Omega)\), \(u>0\) in \(\Omega\), and
\[
\int_\Omega \nabla u\nabla \varphi=\int_\Omega a(x)u^p\varphi
\]
for every \(\varphi\in H^1_0(\Omega)\cap L^\infty(\Omega)\).

Let
\[
S_p(a):=\inf\left\{\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2:\ u\in H^1_0(\Omega),\ \int_\Omega a(x)|u|^{p+1}=1\right\}.
\]
If the embedding \(H^1_0(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{p+1}(\Omega,a(x)dx)\) is compact and \(S_p(a)>0\), then \(S_p(a)\) is achieved by some non-negative function \(w\). By the standard Lagrange multiplier rule, \(w\) satisfies
\[
-\Delta w=S_p(a)a(x)w^p \quad\text{in }\Omega,
\]
and, after the normalization
\[
u=S_p(a)^{\frac1{p-1}}w,
\]
we obtain a positive solution of (2.1).

We shall use the following simple criterion, which is a particular case of the compactness results of the previous section. Assume that
\[
a\in L^r(\Omega),\qquad r\ge 1,
\]
and
\[
\frac1r+\frac{p+1}{2^*}<1
\]
(with the usual convention \(2^*=\infty\) if \(N=1,2\)). Then the functional
\[
u\mapsto \int_\Omega a(x)|u|^{p+1}
\]
is well defined and continuous on \(H^1_0(\Omega)\). Moreover, if the embedding is compact, the above infimum is attained.

In particular, for \(N\ge3\), if
\[
p<\frac{N+2}{N-2}
\]
and \(a\in L^\infty(\Omega)\), the existence follows from the standard Sobolev embedding. In the supercritical case, existence may still hold provided that the weight \(a\) has enough integrability or decay at infinity. More precisely, if
\[
a\in L^r(\Omega)\quad\text{for some }r>\frac{2^*}{2^*-(p+1)},
\]
then the variational problem is well posed and yields a solution whenever the corresponding weighted embedding is compact.

Let $(u_W,u_H)$ be a weak solution corresponding to $f=0$ and $g=0$. Testing the equations with $u_W$ and $u_H$ and integrating over one period, we obtain the energy identity. Since the solution is time-periodic, the time derivative terms vanish after integration over $(0,T)$, and hence
\[
\int_0^T\int_{\Omega_W} |\nabla u_W|^2\,dx\,dt
+
\int_0^T\int_{\Omega_H} |u_H|^2\,dx\,dt
=0.
\]
It follows that $\nabla u_W=0$ in $\Omega_W\times(0,T)$ and $u_H=0$ in $\Omega_H\times(0,T)$. As $\Omega_W$ is connected, $u_W$ is spatially constant on $\Omega_W$ for a.e. $t$. The transmission conditions on $\Gamma$, together with $u_H=0$, imply that this constant is zero. Therefore $u_W=0$ and $u_H=0$, and the weak solution is trivial.

We first state the version of Holmgren's Theorem which will be used in the sequel.

Let $Q$ be an open subset of $\mathbb {R}^{n+1}$ and let
\[
P(x,t,D_x,D_t)=\sum_{|\alpha|+j\leq m}a_{\alpha j}(x,t)D_x^\alpha D_t^j
\]
be a linear differential operator whose coefficients are real analytic in $Q$.  If $u$ is a distribution solution of
\[
P(x,t,D_x,D_t)u=0
\]
in $Q$ and if $u$ vanishes in a nonempty open set on one side of a noncharacteristic hypersurface, then $u$ vanishes in a neighborhood of that hypersurface.  In particular, for the wave operator
\[
\partial_t^2-\Delta
\]
the unique continuation property holds across every noncharacteristic plane.  Thus, if a weak solution of the homogeneous wave equation vanishes in an open subset of space-time, then the vanishing propagates across any plane which is noncharacteristic for the wave operator.

We shall apply this principle as follows.  Suppose that $u$ is a weak solution corresponding to zero data.  The energy identity implies that $u_t=0$ on the observed portion of the boundary, and hence, after using the boundary condition, that $u$ vanishes in a neighborhood of the exterior control region.  By Holmgren's theorem, $u$ must then vanish in the domain of dependence generated by this region.  Repeating the argument and using the geometric condition imposed on the observation set, one obtains
\[
u\equiv 0
\]
throughout the whole cylinder.  This proves uniqueness.

More precisely, the argument is first carried out for smooth solutions, for which the preceding integrations by parts and traces are justified in the classical sense.  The general weak case follows by density, using standard regularization in space and time together with the continuity of the trace and energy norms.  Therefore the only weak solution associated with homogeneous data is the trivial one, and consequently the weak solution of the original problem is unique.

We first prove the following lemma, which is a standard consequence of the Holmgren uniqueness theorem.

\[
\text{If }v\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb {R};H^1_0(\Omega))\quad\text{and}\quad
v_{tt}-\Delta v=0
\]
in a neighborhood of a noncharacteristic hypersurface, and if both \(v\) and its normal derivative vanish on an open portion of that hypersurface, then \(v\) vanishes in a (possibly smaller) neighborhood of that portion.
\]
In particular, for the wave equation, vanishing of the Cauchy data on a nonempty open subset of the lateral boundary propagates locally into the domain.

We now apply this to the present system.  Let \((u,\theta )\) be a weak time-periodic solution corresponding to zero data.  Testing the equations with \(u_t\) and \(\theta\), respectively, and integrating over one time period yields the energy identity
\[
\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega |\nabla \theta |^2\,dx\,dt=0 .
\]
Hence \(\nabla \theta=0\) a.e. in \(\Omega\times(0,T)\).  Since \(\theta=0\) on the boundary, it follows that
\[
\theta\equiv 0\qquad\text{a.e. in }\Omega\times(0,T).
\]
The coupled system therefore reduces to the homogeneous wave equation for \(u\),
\[
u_{tt}-\Delta u=0
\]
in \(\Omega\times(0,T)\), with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition.  Moreover, the boundary coupling implies that the normal trace \(\partial_\nu u\) vanishes on the portion of the boundary where the parabolic variable is observed.  Thus \(u\) has both zero Dirichlet and zero Neumann trace on a nonempty open subset of the lateral boundary.

By the Holmgren uniqueness theorem, \(u\) vanishes in a neighborhood of this boundary portion.  The standard propagation-of-uniqueness/continuation argument for the wave equation then implies that \(u\) vanishes identically in the whole cylinder \(\Omega\times(0,T)\).  Therefore
\[
u\equiv 0,\qquad \theta\equiv 0
\]
a.e. in space-time, and the homogeneous time-periodic weak solution is trivial.  This proves uniqueness.

For every positive integer $n$, we construct a diagram $D_n$ of a split link such that any sequence of Reidemeister moves taking $D_n$ to a split diagram must pass through a diagram with at least $c(D_n)+n$ crossings. Our examples are based on families of hard unknots and use the connection between splitting number and the behavior of diagrammatic isotopies under Reidemeister moves. This gives the first examples of split links whose diagrams are provably hard to split in the sense of requiring an arbitrarily large crossing increase.

In addition, we prove that the conjugacy problem is solvable for extensions of RAAGs by finite groups acting by graph automorphisms, and for several related families obtained by combining length-preserving automorphisms with partial conjugations. Our methods combine normal form arguments for graph products, fixed-point results for finite group actions on $\mathrm{CAT}(0)$ cube complexes, and reductions of conjugacy in finite extensions to twisted conjugacy problems in the RAAG.

We will use the existence of contracting elements, together with the results of \cite{Genevois_conjugacy}, to obtain undecidability of the conjugacy problem in many virtual RAAGs. Recall that an element of a group acting on a metric space is contracting if some (equivalently, any) of its orbits is a contracting quasi-geodesic. In the setting of right-angled Artin groups, such elements are precisely the rank-one elements for the standard action on the universal cover of the Salvetti complex. More generally, in the virtual setting, the same phenomenon can be detected from the action on the associated CAT(0) cube complex.

Our next goal is therefore to establish the existence of contracting elements in the virtual RAAGs under consideration. This will be used as an input for the combination theorem for conjugacy, which reduces the problem to controlling conjugacy inside suitable stabilizers. In particular, once a contracting element is available, the presence of sufficiently complicated subgroups produces examples in which the conjugacy problem is undecidable.

We prove that, for a suitable choice of the parameters $p$ and $q$, the diagrams $\mathcal D(p,q)$ are highly non-split in the sense that any sequence of Reidemeister moves which takes $\mathcal D(p,q)$ to a split diagram must pass through a diagram with many more crossings. More precisely, although the number of crossings of $\mathcal D(p,q)$ is polynomial in $p$ and $q$, the splitting number, measured by the maximal number of crossings appearing along a Reidemeister sequence, grows faster than any prescribed polynomial for appropriate choices of the parameters.

The key point is that the unknot $U$ bounds an embedded disk which is forced to intersect the sublink $M$ in many points during any splitting isotopy. This obstruction is detected by applying the main theorem on the complexity of isotopies of surfaces in the complement of a link. In particular, we obtain lower bounds for the number of Reidemeister moves, and hence for the intermediate crossing number, required to separate the two sublinks of $L(p,q)$.

Thus the diagrams $\mathcal D(p,q)$ give explicit examples of split links admitting diagrams which are hard to split: while the links themselves are split, every simplification to a visibly split diagram necessarily goes through diagrams of very large complexity.

Let $f,g\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2M})$, the Moyal star product is defined by
\[
f\star g=f\exp\left(\frac{i}{2}\overleftarrow{\partial_i}\theta^{ij}\overrightarrow{\partial_j}\right)g
=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{i}{2}\right)^n
\theta^{i_1j_1}\cdots\theta^{i_nj_n}
(\partial_{i_1}\cdots\partial_{i_n}f)(\partial_{j_1}\cdots\partial_{j_n}g).
\]
In particular, the coordinate functions satisfy
\[
[x^i,x^j]_\star=x^i\star x^j-x^j\star x^i=i\theta^{ij}.
\]
The Moyal bracket is defined by
\[
\{f,g\}_\star=\frac{1}{i}(f\star g-g\star f),
\]
which gives a deformation of the canonical Poisson bracket. For polynomial functions the above series terminates whenever one of the factors is of finite degree, and hence the formulas are well defined in the present setting.

The star product is defined by
\[
(f\star g)(x)=f(x)\exp\left(\frac{i}{2}\overleftarrow{\partial_i}\Theta^{ij}\overrightarrow{\partial_j}\right)g(x),
\]
where summation over repeated indices is understood. Equivalently,
\[
(f\star g)(x)=\frac{1}{(\pi\theta)^{2M}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2M}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2M}} f(x+y)g(x+z)e^{-2i y\Theta^{-1}z}\,dy\,dz .
\]
The product is associative and noncommutative, and the coordinates satisfy
\[
[x^\mu,x^\nu]_\star=x^\mu\star x^\nu-x^\nu\star x^\mu=i\Theta^{\mu\nu}.
\]
Moreover, the ordinary integral is a trace on the Moyal algebra:
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2M}} (f\star g)(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2M}} f(x)g(x)\,dx
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2M}} (g\star f)(x)\,dx .
\]
For rapidly decreasing functions the involution is given by complex conjugation,
\[
(f\star g)^*=g^*\star f^* ,
\]
so that the Moyal algebra provides the standard deformation quantization of the symplectic vector space \((\mathbb{R}^{2M},\Theta)\).

A ring $\Re$ is said to be a local ring if it has a unique maximal ideal. A finite commutative principal ideal ring is called a finite chain ring if its ideals are linearly ordered by inclusion. Equivalently, $\Re$ is a finite local principal ideal ring whose maximal ideal is of the form $\langle \gamma\rangle$, where $\gamma$ is a nilpotent element. If the nilpotency index of $\gamma$ is $e$, then the ideals of $\Re$ are
\[
\Re=\langle \gamma^{0}\rangle \supset \langle \gamma\rangle \supset \langle \gamma^{2}\rangle \supset \cdots \supset \langle \gamma^{e-1}\rangle \supset \langle \gamma^{e}\rangle=\{0\}.
\]
The residue field of $\Re$ is defined as $\overline{\Re}=\Re/\langle\gamma\rangle$ and is isomorphic to a finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ for some prime power $q$. Thus $|\Re|=q^{e}$. A set $T$ of representatives of the cosets of $\langle \gamma\rangle$ in $\Re$ is called a Teichm\"uller set, and every element $r\in \Re$ can be written uniquely in the form
\[
r=r_{0}+r_{1}\gamma+\cdots+r_{e-1}\gamma^{e-1},
\]
where $r_{i}\in T$ for $0\leq i\leq e-1$.

We separate the probability that a system admits at least one equilibrium from the conditional distribution of the number and composition of equilibria when they exist. This decomposition yields system-level quantities for feasibility, multiplicity, and diversity that are not recoverable from state-centered summaries alone. We show how the framework unifies questions about the existence of feasible equilibria, the prevalence of alternative stable or admissible configurations, and the distribution of biodiversity across possible outcomes within the same underlying system. By distinguishing absence of admissible states from low multiplicity among systems that do have them, the formalism clarifies how model structure, parameter uncertainty, and ecological constraints shape coexistence patterns. The approach provides a common language for comparing ecological and evolutionary models with multiple equilibria and highlights the importance of accounting for system-level variation when interpreting biodiversity predictions.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:hambl_plateau}
Let $\lambda,\beta>0$. There exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that
\[
        h_{\lambda,\beta}(t)>0,\qquad t\in [0,1-\varepsilon],
\]
and
\[
        h_{\lambda,\beta}(t)=0,\qquad t\in [1-\varepsilon,1].
\]
In particular the minimizer in the variational problem defining
$h_{\lambda,\beta}$ has a terminal plateau, and one may take $T=1$ in
Theorem \ref{thm:main_general}.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By the Euler--Lagrange characterization of minimizers from
Proposition \ref{prop:variational_euler}, the non-contact set is an open
interval on which the optimal path solves the Hamiltonian system
associated with the Legendre transform of the displacement law.  Since the
endpoint constraint is $h(1)=0$ and the obstacle is also equal to zero
there, the complementary slackness condition implies that once the path
touches the obstacle it remains there.  It remains to rule out an isolated
contact at time $1$.

Suppose, to the contrary, that the contact set has empty interior at the
right endpoint.  Then the optimal path is strictly positive on $(0,1)$.
On this interval the first variation vanishes.  Writing
$p(t)=\partial_v I(\dot h(t))$, we obtain
\[
        \dot p(t)=\lambda \beta\, e^{-\lambda h(t)}
\]
in the sense of distributions.  Hence $p$ is strictly increasing.  On the
other hand the transversality condition at the terminal point gives
$p(1^-)\le 0$.  Therefore $p(t)<0$ for all $t<1$, and consequently
$\dot h(t)$ is bounded above by a negative constant on a left-neighbourhood
of $1$, by strict convexity of the log-Laplace transform.  This is
incompatible with $h(t)>0$ and $h(1)=0$ unless the path hits the obstacle
strictly before time $1$.  Thus the contact set contains an interval
$[1-\varepsilon,1]$.

The positivity on $[0,1-\varepsilon)$ follows from the definition of
$\varepsilon$ as the first contact time and from the maximum principle for
the preceding Euler--Lagrange equation.
\end{proof}

\[
\psi\,\Ham(\Sigma,\omega)\,\psi^{-1}=\Ham(\Sigma,\omega').

\[

\begin{defi}
A Riemannian manifold \((M^n,g)\), \(n\geq 3\), is said to carry a
Ricci soliton with potential vector field \(V\) if there exists a constant
\(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:RS}
   \frac12 \mathcal L_V g+\Ric=\lambda g .
\end{equation}
If \(V=\nabla f\), then \((M,g,f,\lambda)\) is called a gradient Ricci
soliton and \eqref{eq:RS} becomes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:GRS}
   \Hess f+\Ric=\lambda g .
\end{equation}
The soliton is shrinking, steady, or expanding according as
\(\lambda>0\), \(\lambda=0\), or \(\lambda<0\).

meaning to nonlinear operations on distributions arising in the analysis of singular

One of the main results of this article, Theorem~\ref{thm:reconstruction}, shows that this is indeed the case under very general assumptions. It states that, given such a coherent family of local expansions, there exists a unique distribution which, close to any given point, is well approximated by the corresponding jet, with an error of the order prescribed by $\gamma$. This result is the analogue, in the present setting, of the classical reconstruction theorem for regularity structures, and is the fundamental tool allowing one to pass from abstract local descriptions to genuine distributions.

The spaces $\CD^\gamma_\alpha$ are therefore the natural domains on which singular operations can be defined. Indeed, while products, compositions, or integrations against singular kernels may be ill-defined at the level of distributions, they can often be performed at the level of the local expansions, where the algebraic structure of the model keeps track of the singular behaviour. The reconstruction theorem then allows one to interpret the result again as an actual distribution. This is the mechanism that will be used throughout the paper to give a robust meaning to the objects appearing in singular stochastic PDEs.

We give a detailed account of the formation of singularities in finite time, and describe the surgery procedure which allows one to continue the flow past singular times. The main result is the existence of the Ricci flow with surgery for all time, with canonical neighborhoods at all sufficiently high curvature points, and with a priori estimates which are uniform under the appropriate choices of parameters.
